TEACHER NOTES:
Lesson 4 of the Fang Fang's Chinese New Year unit. Today's focus is the vocabulary word 'appetite', the opening sentence of a recount, and adjectives in sentences.
2:
TEACHER NOTES:
Orientation slide. Confirm Express or Extended path. No student-facing teaching needed.
3:
TEACHER NOTES:
Teacher preparation reminder. Best read before the lesson, not during.
4:
TEACHER NOTES:
Icon legend for I Do, We Do, CFU and You Do. Skim only.
5:
TEACHER NOTES:
Engagement icon legend. Skim only.
6:
TEACHER NOTES:
Story grammar icon legend. Skim only. Today's recount work uses the when, where, what, who icons for the opening sentence.
7:
TEACHER NOTES:
Colour coding chart for grammar referencing. Skim only.
8:
SAY:
- "Today we need a pencil, a mini whiteboard with a texta, and our booklet."
- "Put them on your desk so we can start."

DO:
- Hold up each item as you say it.
- Wait until each student has them ready.

TEACHER NOTES:
Quick setup. Keep under 30 seconds.

WATCH FOR:
- Students still searching when teaching starts. Pause and reset.
9:
TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider for vocabulary. The focus word is 'appetite'. Move on to the routine slide.
10:
SOURCES:
Collins Primary School Dictionary, https://schools.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/primary, accessed 8.2.26

SAY:
- "Our word today is appetite."
- "Say it with me. Appetite."
- "An appetite is a desire to eat."
- "In the story, Fang Fang's aunt said Lisa had a good appetite because she tried all the different foods."
- "After running, you might have a bigger appetite. When you are growing, your appetite gets bigger too."

DO:
- Point to the word as you say it.
- Have students choral say it three times.
- Use a 'rub tummy' action when you say it.

TEACHER NOTES:
Follow the four-part vocabulary routine. The word is abstract, so anchor it with the tummy action and Lisa's example.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who say 'apple' or 'appletite'. Slow the word down and have them try again.
11:
SAY:
- "Fang Fang's aunt said Lisa had a good appetite."
- "Ask: what did Lisa do that showed a good appetite? Expected: she tried all the different Chinese foods."
- "Show me with the rub tummy action."

DO:
- Read the slide aloud.
- Take a quick choral response.
- Connect back to the read aloud where Lisa eats the duck and the dumplings.

TEACHER NOTES:
This slide unpacks the story example. Students must remember Lisa tried the food, even though she was new to it.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who think Lisa did not eat. Remind them she ate the duck and the dumpling.
12:
SAY:
- "Which words are similar to appetite?"
- "Ask: hunger? Expected: yes."
- "Ask: full? Expected: no."
- "Ask: sleepy? Expected: no."
- "Show me thumbs up if it is similar."

DO:
- Take one word at a time.
- Cue thumbs after each.
- Reveal the answer by repeating the meaning each time.

TEACHER NOTES:
Quick synonym check. 'Hunger' is the closest synonym for Foundation. 'Full' is the opposite. 'Sleepy' is unrelated.

WATCH FOR:
- Students saying 'full' is similar. Reteach: full is when your tummy is done. Appetite is when you want to eat.
13:
SAY:
- "Appetite means how hungry you feel."
- "I will read each question. You answer yes or no."
- "Ask: can you have a big appetite after running? Expected: yes."
- "Ask: if you feel full, do you still have a big appetite? Expected: no."
- "Ask: can you lose your appetite when you feel sick? Expected: yes."
- "Ask: does appetite mean the same as thirsty? Expected: no."
- "Ask: can your appetite change during the day? Expected: yes."

DO:
- Read each question one at a time.
- Cue a yes/no response (thumbs or choral).
- Connect to students' own experiences if helpful.

TEACHER NOTES:
Five-question check. Each question pushes the meaning a bit further. If a question stumps students, slow down and explain.

WATCH FOR:
- Students confusing 'appetite' with 'thirsty'. Mime drinking versus eating.
14:
SAY:
- "Look at the pictures."
- "Ask: which image shows someone with a good appetite? Expected: the person eating lots of food, looking hungry."
- "Show me with your finger pointing."

DO:
- Point to each image.
- Take a response.
- Ask one student why they chose that picture.

TEACHER NOTES:
Visual check. Foundation students should reason from what they see.

WATCH FOR:
- Students choosing because they like the food in the picture. Redirect to 'who looks hungry?'
15:
SAY:
- "After playing soccer all afternoon, Mia had a big appetite."
- "Ask: did she say she felt sick, or ask for more food? Expected: ask for more food."
- "Show me on your fingers, one for sick, two for ask for more food."

DO:
- Cover the answer until students show fingers.
- Reveal the answer.
- Ask one student why.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Me Fingers
Script:
- Ask: did Mia say she felt sick or ask for more food? Expected: ask for more food.
- Scan for: most fingers showing 2.
PROCEED:
- >=80% show 2. Move to recount work.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students think 'big appetite' means feeling sick.
- Reteach: do the rub tummy action and say 'big appetite means I want to eat lots'.
- Re-check: ask 'after a long run, do you want food or no food?' Expected: food.

TEACHER NOTES:
Threshold check for vocabulary. If many miss, do a quick reteach before recount work.

WATCH FOR:
- Students with mixed fingers. Take one of each and ask 'why?'
16:
TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider for understanding, responding to and creating text. The next slides build the opening sentence of a recount.
17:
SAY:
- "Let's listen to the recount about Chinese New Year again."
- "As I read each part, do the action for the matching icon."
- "Listen and watch."

DO:
- Read the mentor recount aloud (Last week, we went to Chinatown... I felt proud and happy).
- Pause after each sentence so students can do the matching action (when, where, who, events, feeling).
- Praise students using the right action at the right time.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note covers this. The recount is the bridge to the opening sentence focus. Keep it moving.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who freeze on actions. Pair them with a confident neighbour.
18:
SAY:
- "Listen carefully to the first sentence."
- "Last week, we went to Chinatown with my family to celebrate the Chinese New Year."
- "This is the opening sentence."
- "It tells us when, where, what, and who."

DO:
- Choral read the sentence with students.
- Point to the words 'opening sentence'.
- Use the icon actions as you say each part (when = clock action, where = around the room, what = pointing at events, who = pointing to people).

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note suggests choral reading the opening sentence. Use the icon actions to reinforce that the opening sentence holds four pieces of information.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who think only one icon is in the sentence. Show that all four fit in one sentence.
19:
SAY:
- "Look at the opening sentence again."
- "Ask: which words tell us when? Expected: last week."
- "Ask: which words tell us where? Expected: Chinatown."
- "Ask: which words tell us what? Expected: celebrate the Chinese New Year."
- "Ask: which words tell us who? Expected: my family."

DO:
- Highlight or point to each part as students name it.
- Use the icon action for each (when, where, what, who).
- Choral read the sentence again at the end.

TEACHER NOTES:
This slide unpacks the opening sentence into the four icons. Strong visual model for the You Do task later.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who muddle the parts. Slow down and re-read with the actions.
20:
SAY:
- "Listen to two sentences."
- "I went camping with my family."
- "At Easter, I go camping in the bush with my family."
- "Ask: which is a better opening sentence? Expected: the second one (At Easter, I go camping in the bush with my family)."
- "Ask: why? Expected: it tells us when, where, what and who."

DO:
- Read both sentences aloud.
- Point to each detail in the second sentence using the icons.
- Compare what the first sentence is missing.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: discuss the difference between each sentence. The first is missing 'when' and 'where'. Make this concrete using the icons.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick the shorter sentence because it is easier. Affirm but redirect to 'which one tells us more?'
21:
SAY:
- "Look at the picture."
- "Two opening sentences are on the slide."
- "On my last birthday, my family and I went to the beach."
- "I celebrated my birthday with my family."
- "Ask: which is the better opening sentence for this celebration? Expected: the first one (On my last birthday, my family and I went to the beach)."
- "Ask: why? Expected: it tells us where (the beach)."

DO:
- Read both sentences aloud.
- Use the icon actions.
- Take responses on whiteboards or fingers.
- Reveal the answer and explain.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Me Fingers
Script:
- Ask: which is the better opening sentence, one or two? Expected: 1.
- Scan for: most fingers showing 1.
PROCEED:
- >=80% show 1. Move to the You Do practice.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students choose the shorter sentence.
- Reteach: walk through each icon (when, where, what, who) and tick which sentence has it.
- Re-check: ask 'which sentence tells us where?' Expected: the first one (the beach).

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: 'second sentence is missing the where detail'. This is the threshold check before students try their own opening sentence.

WATCH FOR:
- Students with mixed fingers. Take one of each and ask 'why?'
22:
SAY:
- "Now you will plan your own opening sentence."
- "Use the question prompts."
- "Start with when. When did your celebration happen?"
- "Then where, what, and who."

DO:
- Read each question aloud.
- Point to the icon and the matching question.
- Have students think silently for 30 seconds.
- Tell them to start with the 'when' detail.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: prompt students to start with the 'when' detail. This slide gives the question scaffold for the booklet task.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who jump straight to 'what'. Bring them back to 'when first'.
23:
SAY:
- "Use the word bank if you need ideas."
- "For when, you might say on Saturday, on Lunar New Year, or on my birthday."
- "For where, you might say at home, at the park, or at a restaurant."
- "For what, you might say had, went to, or celebrated."
- "For who, you might say me, my family, or my friends."

DO:
- Read each part of the word bank aloud.
- Point to each option as you read.
- Tell students they can borrow these words or use their own.

TEACHER NOTES:
This word bank is a scaffold. Use it for students who freeze on planning their sentence.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who copy the word bank without thinking about their celebration. Prompt them to choose a word that matches their picture.
24:
SAY:
- "Find your celebration drawing in your booklet."
- "Draw a picture to match your opening sentence."
- "Make sure your picture shows when, where, what and who."

DO:
- Direct students to the booklet page.
- Walk around and check picture details.
- Prompt with 'where is the when in your picture?' if details are missing.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: Sit beside the student and place an icon at a time, asking them what to draw for that icon.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: Add labels next to the people, place, and event in the picture.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is the You Do drawing for the opening sentence. Students will refer back to this picture in Lesson 5 (detail sentences) and Lesson 6 (final sentence).

WATCH FOR:
- Students who finish in 30 seconds with one stick figure. Prompt them to add the place and the event.
25:
SAY:
- "Practise saying your opening sentence with a partner."
- "Point to each part of your picture as you say the sentence."
- "Then swap with your partner."

DO:
- Pair students up.
- Listen in to a few pairs.
- Invite a few students to share with the class.
- Praise students who include all four parts (when, where, what, who).

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: students rehearse with a partner before sharing with the class. This is essential rehearsal for Lessons 5 and 6.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who skip a part. Whisper-prompt 'what about the when?'
- Students who freeze. Read the prompt question for them.
26:
TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider for sentence-level writing. The focus is adjectives in sentences. This builds on the work from Lesson 3.
27:
SAY:
- "Remember, an adjective is a word that tells us more about a noun."
- "It describes what a noun is like."
- "Adjectives can tell us about size, colour, shape, age, or quality."
- "Say it with me. Adjective."

DO:
- Read the slide aloud.
- Use the paint brush action from Lesson 3.
- Have students choral say 'adjective tells us more about a noun'.

TEACHER NOTES:
Quick I Do revision of adjectives. Most students will remember from Lesson 3. Keep brief.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who can say the word but not the meaning. Use the paint brush action to anchor it.
28:
SAY:
- "Read the sentence with me. The children carried glowing lanterns."
- "Ask: which word tells us more about the lanterns? Expected: glowing."
- "The word 'glowing' is the adjective."

DO:
- Choral read the sentence.
- Point to the noun (lanterns) first, then the adjective (glowing).
- Use the paint brush action on 'glowing'.

TEACHER NOTES:
The slide title says 'Which word tells us more about the moon?' but the sentence is about lanterns. Treat the sentence as the source. The adjective is 'glowing' and the noun is 'lanterns'. Read the title as 'lanterns' if needed for Foundation students.

WATCH FOR:
- Students confused by the title saying 'moon'. Redirect them to the actual sentence.
29:
SAY:
- "Read the sentence with me. Lisa tasted the yummy dumpling."
- "Ask: what are the nouns? Expected: Lisa, dumpling."
- "Ask: what word tells us more about the dumpling? Expected: yummy."
- "Yummy is the adjective."

DO:
- Choral read the sentence.
- Point to each noun.
- Point to the adjective.
- Use the paint brush action.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note mentions 'old' and 'path' but the sentence is about 'yummy' and 'dumpling'. Use the sentence on the slide. This is We Do practice for finding adjectives.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who name 'tasted' as the adjective. Remind them adjectives describe nouns, not actions.
30:
SAY:
- "Read the sentence with me. The colourful firecrackers exploded."
- "Ask: what is the adjective? Expected: colourful."
- "Show me by pointing to the word."

DO:
- Choral read the sentence.
- Point to 'firecrackers' (noun), then 'colourful' (adjective).
- Use the paint brush action.

TEACHER NOTES:
We Do practice. The adjective comes before the noun, like usual. Connect to the firecrackers in the read aloud.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who say 'exploded' as the adjective. Remind them adjectives describe a thing, not an action.
31:
SAY:
- "Read the sentence with me. The bright dragon twisted through the street."
- "Ask: what is the adjective? Expected: bright."
- "Show me on your fingers, one for dragon, two for bright, three for twisted."

DO:
- Cover the answer until students show fingers.
- Reveal the answer.
- Ask one student why bright is the adjective.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Me Fingers
Script:
- Ask: which word is the adjective, dragon, bright, or twisted? Expected: bright.
- Scan for: most fingers showing 2.
PROCEED:
- >=80% show 2. Move on to adding adjectives.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students pick 'twisted' because it is the action.
- Reteach: show that adjectives describe a thing, not an action. Use 'bright dragon' versus 'dragon twisted'.
- Re-check: ask 'which word tells us about the dragon?' Expected: bright.

TEACHER NOTES:
Threshold check before moving to adding adjectives.

WATCH FOR:
- Students with mixed fingers. Take one of each and ask 'why?'
32:
SAY:
- "Listen to this sentence. Fang Fang wore a dress."
- "We can make this sentence more detailed by adding an adjective."
- "Ask: what adjective could describe the dress? Expected: blue."
- "Now the sentence becomes: Fang Fang wore a blue dress."

DO:
- Read the original sentence.
- Take a few adjective ideas.
- Read the new expanded sentence with 'blue'.
- Have students choral repeat the new sentence.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: model adding an adjective. This is I Do for sentence expansion.

WATCH FOR:
- Students adding the adjective in the wrong place. Remind them the adjective comes before the noun.
33:
SAY:
- "Listen to this sentence. The waiter brought over vegetables."
- "Ask: what adjective could describe the vegetables? Expected: colourful."
- "Now the sentence becomes: The waiter brought over colourful vegetables."

DO:
- Read the original sentence.
- Take a few adjective ideas.
- Read the new expanded sentence with 'colourful'.
- Have students choral repeat.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: model adding an adjective. Second I Do example so students hear the pattern.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who suggest a verb instead of an adjective. Use the paint brush test.
34:
SAY:
- "Look at the picture and listen. Lisa tasted the duck."
- "Ask: what adjectives can we use to describe the duck? Expected: tasty, warm, steaming, delicious."
- "Let's expand the sentence. Lisa tasted the warm duck."

DO:
- Read the original sentence.
- Take adjective ideas from students.
- Read the new expanded sentence with one chosen adjective.
- Have students choral repeat.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: read the sentence, find the noun, brainstorm, expand, re-read, state the adjective. Follow the routine.

WATCH FOR:
- Students suggesting adjectives that do not fit the picture. Affirm but redirect to a fitting one.
35:
SAY:
- "Listen to the sentence. They heard a bang."
- "Ask: what adjectives can we use to describe the bang? Expected: big, scary, loud, frightening."
- "Let's expand the sentence. They heard a loud bang."

DO:
- Follow the same routine: read, brainstorm, expand, re-read.
- Use the paint brush action on the chosen adjective.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: same routine. Connect to the firecrackers in the read aloud.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who freeze on a sound word. Prompt with 'is it loud or quiet?'
36:
SAY:
- "Listen to the sentence. They sat down in the restaurant."
- "Ask: what adjectives can we use to describe the restaurant? Expected: busy, crowded, loud, noisy."
- "Let's expand the sentence. They sat down in the busy restaurant."

DO:
- Follow the same routine.
- Use the paint brush action on the chosen adjective.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: same routine. Third example, students should be picking up the pattern.

WATCH FOR:
- Students using the same adjective every time. Push for a fresh one.
37:
SAY:
- "Look at the picture of the dragon."
- "Ask: which adjective best describes the dragon, dull, bright, or boring? Expected: bright."
- "Show me on your fingers, one for dull, two for bright, three for boring."

DO:
- Cover the answer until students show fingers.
- Reveal the answer.
- Ask one student why bright fits the dragon.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Me Fingers
Script:
- Ask: which adjective best describes the dragon, dull, bright, or boring? Expected: bright.
- Scan for: most fingers showing 2.
PROCEED:
- >=80% show 2. Move to the You Do class activity.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students pick 'dull' or 'boring' because the words sound similar.
- Reteach: show the dragon picture and ask 'is it dull or bright?' using the contrast.
- Re-check: ask 'is the sun dull or bright?' Expected: bright.

TEACHER NOTES:
Threshold check before the You Do activity.

WATCH FOR:
- Students with mixed fingers. Take one of each and ask 'why?'
38:
SAY:
- "Now we will play match the adjective to the noun."
- "When I say an adjective, walk to the picture of the noun that matches."
- "Then say a sentence using both."
- "For example, if I say sparkly, you might walk to the firecrackers and say 'The sparkly firecrackers made a bang.'"

DO:
- Place the noun pictures around the room (lantern, dragon, firecrackers, lion, chopsticks, dumplings).
- Call out an adjective from the next slide bank.
- Watch students move.
- After each round, say a sample sentence.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: Offer two adjectives at a time and ask students to pick the better fit (e.g., is the restaurant busy or quiet?).
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: Ask students to suggest another adjective for the same noun and say a fresh sentence orally.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note covers this. This is the You Do class activity. Keep the pace moving so every student gets at least two turns.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who copy a friend rather than think. Stand near them and prompt the choice.
39:
SAY:
- "Use these adjectives in our class activity."
- "You might hear: bright, fierce, glowing, long, colourful, dazzling, big, loud, vibrant, noisy, shiny, majestical, delicate, red, glossy."

DO:
- Read the adjective bank aloud.
- Choose adjectives that fit the noun pictures you have placed.
- Use as many or as few as time allows.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: use as many or as few as needed. This is the prompt bank for the teacher to draw from.

WATCH FOR:
- Students puzzled by 'majestical' or 'dazzling'. Briefly define these as 'looks amazing' for Foundation.
40:
SAY:
- "If you need help thinking of an adjective, look at these picture cards."
- "Ask: what is each picture doing or feeling?"

DO:
- Display the cards as needed.
- Use them only with students who freeze.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: optional scaffold. Use only if students need extra support to generate adjectives.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who use a card every round without thinking. Push them to try without first.
41:
TEACHER NOTES:
Closing credits slide. No teaching needed. Save the celebration drawings for Lessons 5 and 6.
